title: Planned obsolescence

definition.text: Designing a product with an artificially short useful life or a deliberately weak design so that it stops working, or looks out of date, after a set time.

facts.text: The aim is to boost long-term sales by shortening the time between repeat purchases, the 'replacement cycle'.
It works best when a producer has at least an oligopoly, and relies on the buyer not knowing how long the product was designed to last.
Product lifespans tend to rise as markets become more competitive, as when longer-lasting Japanese cars pushed American carmakers to build more durable vehicles.
In the 1920s General Motors' Alfred P. Sloan Jr. introduced yearly model changes to keep car sales up in a saturated market.
In 2015 France set fines of up to €300,000 and up to two years in jail for planning product failure, the first legislature to recognize the practice.
In the US it is being tackled through state right-to-repair laws.
Supporters such as Philip Kotler see it as competition and technology at work, while critics such as Vance Packard call it wasteful and exploitative.

contested_note: Supporters see shortened replacement cycles as a product of competition and innovation, critics as waste and exploitation of customers.

definition.text: The different ways products are made to become obsolete, from built-in short lifetimes to deliberate disabling.

facts.text: Contrived durability shortens a product's life before release by designing it to wear out quickly, for example with inferior materials in critical parts.
Prevention of repairs makes goods hard or uneconomic to fix, such as glued-in components or overpriced spare parts.
Programmed obsolescence deliberately disables a working product, such as ink cartridge chips that stop use while ink remains.

definition.text: When products still work but seem out of date because styles change, so buyers replace them.

facts.text: It arises from consumer perception rather than from a designer's plan.
Fashion goods such as clothing go through a 'fashion cycle' that manufacturers ride with new designs while old ones still work.

definition.text: Using the Earth's limited resources sustainably so that the same output or consumption is achieved with fewer resources and less environmental impact.

facts.text: Improvements can happen at the production, consumption and end-of-life stages of a product.
Its measures and aims closely resemble those of resource productivity, resource intensity and eco-efficiency.
A key tool is measuring resource use, such as carbon, water and land footprints, and finding the 'hot spots' where most is used or most can be saved.
A resource-efficient Europe was one of seven flagship initiatives of the EU's Europe 2020 strategy.
The European Commission noted trade-offs: green vehicles cut fossil fuel use but add pressure on electricity, rare-earth elements and lithium.

definition.text: The amount of a resource, such as water, energy or materials, needed to produce, process and dispose of one unit of a good or service.

facts.text: Nationally it can be calculated as units of resource used per unit of GDP.
High resource intensity means a high price or environmental cost of turning resources into GDP.
It is the mirror image of resource productivity: resource use per unit of outcome rather than outcome per unit of resource; the goal is to minimize intensity and maximize productivity.
The OECD and UNEP use resource intensity indicators to track progress in decoupling growth from environmental damage.

definition.text: The amount of a good or service obtained for each unit of resource used.

facts.text: It can be expressed as money earned per unit of resource, such as 'crop per drop' of irrigation water.
With resource intensity, it is a key measure of attempts to decouple resource use from environmental degradation.
Research by Joachim Spangenberg suggests a transition focused on resource productivity gives higher growth than business as usual while easing environmental pressure.

definition.text: Established ways of moving toward sustainability, classically the three strategies of sufficiency, efficiency and consistency.

facts.text: Joseph Huber introduced the original triad of sufficiency, efficiency and consistency.
Sufficiency cuts consumption and production without threatening human needs and is linked to degrowth.
Efficiency cuts resource use, energy or pollution per unit of output within existing systems and has an affinity with green growth.
Consistency shifts to industrial metabolisms more in tune with nature's, such as renewable energy and circular design, and is rooted in industrial ecology.
Maria Sandberg distinguishes four types of sufficiency: absolute reduction, modal shifts, sharing and longer product life.

definition.text: Eric Hartmann's framework of ten sustainability strategies, five for future generations and five for people living today.

facts.text: The five intergenerational strategies add population reduction and regeneration expansion, such as reforestation, to sufficiency, efficiency and consistency.
The five intragenerational strategies are capability empowerment, equalization, eco-efficiency increase, impact expansion and population reduction.
Sustainability is achieved when everyone can meet fundamental needs while environmental impacts stay within safe limits.
